front: How does CSMA/CA avoid collisions?
back: A station listens, waits a random backoff once the channel is quiet, transmits, then expects an ACK. No ACK means it retries.

front: Why is Wi-Fi half duplex?
back: A radio cannot transmit and receive on the same channel at the same time, so stations take turns.

front: Which 2.4 GHz channels do not overlap at 20 MHz width?
back: 1, 6 and 11, the standard plan where channels 1–11 are allowed.

front: Why do neighboring 2.4 GHz channel numbers overlap?
back: Their centers are 5 MHz apart, but each channel is about 20 MHz wide.

front: 2.4 GHz versus 5 GHz: range and channels?
back: 2.4 GHz reaches farther but has only three nonoverlapping channels. 5 GHz has many more channels and a shorter range.

front: What does bonding 5 GHz channels into one 80 MHz channel cost?
back: It uses four 20 MHz channels, so fewer nonoverlapping channels remain for neighboring APs.

front: What must an AP do on a 5 GHz DFS channel?
back: Listen for radar before using the channel, and move to another channel if radar appears.

front: Which security modes can a 6 GHz WLAN use?
back: WPA3 or Enhanced Open (OWE). WPA2 is not allowed at 6 GHz.

front: What do +3 dB and +10 dB do to power?
back: +3 dB doubles it; +10 dB multiplies it by ten.

front: dB versus dBm versus dBi?
back: dB is a ratio. dBm is power relative to 1 mW (0 dBm = 1 mW). dBi is antenna gain relative to an isotropic antenna.

front: Which signal is stronger, −55 dBm or −75 dBm, and by how much?
back: −55 dBm, by 20 dB, which is 100 times the power. Closer to zero is stronger.

front: Signal is −65 dBm and noise is −92 dBm at the same receiver. What is the SNR?
back: 27 dB: signal minus noise, −65 − (−92).

front: Omnidirectional versus directional antenna?
back: Omnidirectional spreads energy in every horizontal direction. Directional (patch, Yagi, dish) concentrates it one way for longer reach.

front: Which bands do 802.11b/g, 802.11a/ac and 802.11n/ax use?
back: b and g: 2.4 GHz. a and ac: 5 GHz. n and ax: both.

front: What is Wi-Fi 6E?
back: 802.11ax operating in the 6 GHz band.

front: PHY rate versus throughput?
back: PHY rate is the speed of the radio link. Throughput is lower because of overhead, retries and shared airtime.

front: SSID versus BSSID?
back: The SSID is the WLAN name, up to 32 bytes. The BSSID is the 48-bit identifier of one BSS, in MAC-address form.

front: BSS versus ESS?
back: A BSS is one AP and its associated clients. An ESS is several BSSs with the same SSID, joined by a distribution system.

front: What is an IBSS?
back: An independent BSS, or ad hoc network: stations communicate directly, with no AP.

front: Co-channel versus adjacent-channel interference?
back: Co-channel: same channel, so stations take turns. Adjacent-channel: overlapping channels, so frames are damaged and resent.

front: Name two common sources of non-Wi-Fi interference at 2.4 GHz.
back: Microwave ovens and Bluetooth devices. Cordless phones and wireless cameras are others.

front: A client shows a strong signal but cannot reach a server. What does signal strength not tell you?
back: Whether airtime is free, the security settings match and the IP settings are valid.

front: Which encryption do WEP, WPA and WPA2 use?
back: WEP: RC4. WPA: TKIP, also based on RC4. WPA2: AES-CCMP.

front: What does WPA3-Personal change from WPA2-Personal?
back: SAE replaces the PSK exchange, and Protected Management Frames (PMF) are required.

front: Personal mode versus Enterprise mode?
back: Personal: everyone shares one passphrase. Enterprise: each user authenticates with 802.1X and EAP, checked by a RADIUS server.
